nameStory: This plant gets its name from its perfectly round leaflets and its habit of sprawling along the ground rather than standing tall. The 'tick-trefoil' part comes from its notorious seeds that stick to your clothes and pet fur like tiny ticks, though thankfully these plant hitchhikers are completely harmless!
description: Round-leaved Trailing Tick-trefoil is a low-growing member of the pea family that hugs the ground with trailing stems. It rarely grows more than a foot tall, instead spreading outward with wiry stems that can stretch 2-3 feet long. The plant produces small pink to purple pea-like flowers in late summer, followed by flat, segmented seed pods that are covered in tiny hooked hairs.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three perfectly round leaflets per leaf, each about the size of a quarter, with a soft, velvety texture when you rub them between your fingers

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Sprawling, trailing stems that hug the ground and root at joints where they touch soil, creating a mat-like appearance

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny pink to purple pea-shaped flowers, about 1/4 inch long, clustered on short upright spikes that rise above the trailing stems in late summer

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Flat, jointed seed pods that break apart into triangular segments covered in hooked hairs that grab onto fabric and fur with remarkable tenacity

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thin, wiry stems covered in fine hairs that feel slightly rough to the touch and often have a reddish tinge

habitat: Look for this ground-hugger in dry, sandy soils of open woodlands, forest edges, and clearings throughout New England. It thrives in partially shaded areas where the soil is well-drained, often growing alongside other low woodland plants like wintergreen and wild sarsaparilla.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as small, rounded leaflets on trailing stems. The plant is still developing its full sprawling habit at this time.
seasonality.summer: The characteristic round leaflets are fully developed and easy to spot. Late summer brings the small pink-purple flowers on short upright spikes.
seasonality.fall: Seeds mature and become incredibly sticky, making this the best time to experience their famous hitchhiking abilities. Leaves may turn yellowish before dropping.
seasonality.winter: Only the woody stem bases remain visible above ground, though the extensive root system survives to regrow next spring.

funFact: The hooked hairs on tick-trefoil seeds are so perfectly designed that they inspired the invention of Velcro - Swiss engineer George de Mestral studied these and similar seeds under a microscope after picking them off his dog's fur during a 1941 hiking trip!
confusionNotes: The round leaflets make this nearly impossible to confuse with other tick-trefoils, which have oval or elongated leaflets. The only real confusion might be with young poison ivy, but poison ivy leaflets are never perfectly round and the plant lacks the trailing, mat-forming habit.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the intimidating name, tick-trefoils have nothing to do with actual ticks - the name simply refers to how the seeds 'tick' onto your clothing. These plants are actually beneficial nitrogen-fixers that improve soil quality in their woodland homes.
compareHints: Among the tick-trefoils, this is the only one with perfectly round leaflets and a distinctly trailing growth habit. Most other tick-trefoils in New England grow upright and have oval or lance-shaped leaflets. The combination of round leaves and ground-hugging stems makes this species unmistakable within its genus.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its tick-trefoil relatives, showy tick-trefoil is typically the tallest and most robust, with the largest and most densely packed flower clusters.

Among New England's many ticktrefoils, panicled ticktrefoil stands out with its distinctly narrow, lance-shaped leaflets - much thinner than the broad leaflets of showy tick-trefoil or the rounded leaves of round-leaved trailing tick-trefoil.
Among the tick-trefoils, this species stands out for its height and smooth appearance.
Among New England's tick-trefoils, Maryland tick-trefoil is distinguished by its relatively small, smooth leaflets and delicate overall appearance.
Among its tick-trefoil relatives, little-leaf stands out for its distinctly smaller leaflets and notably hairy stems.
Among New England's tick-trefoils, perplexed tick-trefoil is most easily confused with tall tick-trefoil, requiring expert examination to separate reliably.
Among its tick-trefoil relatives, the toothed variety stands out for its distinctly serrated leaf edges - most other species have smooth or only slightly toothed leaflets.
Among New England's tick-trefoils, hoary tick-trefoil is the gray ghost - its fuzzy, grayish appearance makes it unmistakable.
Among New England's ticktrefoils, sessileleaf is the only one with leaves that attach directly to the stem without stalks - all its relatives have obvious leaf stems.
Among the tick-trefoils, stiff tick-trefoil stands out for its rigid, unbending stems - most others like showy tick-trefoil or panicled tick-trefoil have flexible stems that sway easily.
